utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Barney Thomas, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. You can call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated. Just to remind you, Major General, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. THE COURT: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before I ask you any questions, sir, I just want to make sure that I can be heard by the various translators, because this is a room in which I sometimes have troubles with the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I can get some affirmation with regard to people being able to hear me, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can hear you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We left our conversation last night discussing that Jackson was under national command. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to that particular issue, I'd like to expand it for a moment, if I could, and discuss with you, if I understand it properly, the principle of unity of command. And I take it that's a principle you're aware of; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, as I am equally aware of the associated principle of unity of effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you have me there. And with regard to the issue of unity of command, could you kindly explain to the Chamber what that principle is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unity of command is a principle that serves to provide coherence to either a national or multinational force. It involves, as far as possible, the use of a common doctrine, an approach to operations, and, more particularly, a clear chain of -- chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the clear chain of command, part of what we were discussing yesterday was that the clear chain of command for Jackson ultimately rested within the British military?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've mentioned another notion, and I don't want to leave you alone with that, and since it's of some importance to you. What is the associated principle of unity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The associated principle of unity of effort is to ensure that the activities or actions of a joint, combined, or multinational force are directed towards a common -- a common aim or a common objective, unity of effort. So it's associated to unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understood. Now, I want to see if I can understand, for purposes of our discussion, a couple of general ideas, and one of them has to do with the notion of misinformation as a tool of war. So my first question to you is -- my first question to you is: With regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- General Melvin is here appearing as an expert, and my concern is that my colleague is now going to an area that is beyond his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe I'll be able to tie it up with a question or two, and I don't believe I'm going beyond his expertise at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In what way, Mr. Saxon, is Mr. Guy-Smith going beyond the expertise of the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, nothing in the four corners of General Melvin's report or the questions that were asked of him relate to misinformation or the use of misinformation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is true, but can that then come under the rubric of lack of expertise in this topic or does it come under any other rubric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is your ground of objection, then, appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is -- well, I will take your point. I would say it does -- it may fall under the ground of lack of expertise, and it certainly falls beyond the scope of General Melvin's report and what he was asked to do. He was not asked to comment about issues of misinformation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the basis of your objection relevance or the lack of expertise in the question asked? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying that a military expert would not have knowledge of whether or not misinformation does get used as a tool of war or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to withdraw that objection. I'm hearing you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have my question in mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question, sir, was: Does misinformation get used as a tool of war? Or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The more common military term which I'm familiar with is the term "deception." And under that heading of "deception," which seeks -- "deception" seeks to confuse one's opponent, to deny him an insight into your plans, and to put him off balance, misinformation could - and I believe does - belong under the general heading of "deception."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Using your term, then, "deception," which I'm happy to adopt, when a commander receives information from sources other than through his own chain of command, is the question of whether or not the information that is received, one that falls into this general rubric of deception, one of the considerations which is taken into account when analysing the information received?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an estimate of the situation, a commander and staff at any headquarters, certainly at a headquarters -- a higher-formation headquarters, will review the information they receive particularly with a view -- the information they've been receiving, particularly their assessment of enemy strengths, dispositions, and assessed intentions, may be designed to mislead and, therefore, would come under "deception."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just go back to a question that Mr. Guy-Smith asked you earlier, when he still used the word "misinformation." Do you agree with that question that he raised, that then deception, to use your term, is used as a tool of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm noting your answer with regard to the question of deception and the kinds of areas. I take it that it goes beyond issues of enemy strength, dispositions, and assessed intentions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only giving you some examples of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- those areas in which intelligence staffs would advise their commander to look at. This is part of the normal military estimate process. And to clarify, in that process, one, through training and experience, looks out for potential areas where a deception might be occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And with regard to one of the areas where a deception might be occurring, and you've mentioned on a couple of occasions in your testimony that we've moved into, I think it would be fair to say, a new technological age where information is moving much more quickly, you used, for example, e-mails, is what you'd referred to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that - if I recall correctly - was in the context in clarifying a point raised by the Judge over the powers of discipline from a -- as far as I can recall from my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. It was the Commonwealth [overlapping speaker] --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I'm taking it in a slightly different area for the moment to see whether this is accurate or not, which is: One of -- one of the areas or one of the features of war has become, in a way, different from days gone by because of technology is news reporting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think news reporting has been a very important aspect of warfare, certainly since the Crimean War.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, once again, you know much better than I do in this regard. And with regard to the issue of news reporting, this is also an area where forces or a commander would have to engage in an analysis with regard to the question of deception as to whether or not the information that is being promulgated through the news is accurate information or not. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very fair statement. Certainly, in my own experience, in any military operation, or planning of operation, one has to take into account the perception -- public perception, that which is reported in the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the whole issue, when trying to understand the accuracy of information that's received, I take it that one of the things that a commander would do, and I'm asking, once again, is -- would rely upon the intelligence information that was promulgated by their own forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a very important source of information, but not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, understood. And when there's a contradiction because of this issue of deception, I'm sure there's no hard-and-fast rule as to -- as to how determinations are made, but it would be more likely than not that in such a situation a commander would rely on the intelligence received from his own sources internally, that information, would it not? I'm asking as a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general proposition, and I'm not an expert on intelligence, but I would -- from my own recollection, it's very important, in assessing information, intelligence, to rely on as many -- or to use and assess as many sources as possible. But within that, clearly, as I think you, yourself, have indicated, one would apply a particular emphasis on one's own intelligence sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when dealing with, for example, and once again going back to -- well, no, we won't go back to that. When dealing with a decision, in the multinational force context, whether or not to red-card or not, and I'll ask you for a definition of red-carding in a second, whether or not to red-card or not, the reliance would be on one's own forces in determining whether or not to take a particular action or not? And before you answer the question, you should probably define "red-card," because I put a term in that I don't think we've discussed, but I read in your report which is --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it assist you if I tried to clarify what I meant by red-carding first?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Red-carding" is a non-doctrinal term that is used widely within the military domain. It tries to express the eventuality or potential eventuality that a national contingent commander, in certain circumstances, might feel that he cannot carry out the orders of a multinational commander. There are potentially, you know, three circumstances -- at least three circumstances in which that could happen. Firstly, he could, inverted commas, "red-card," inverted commas, a task or omission, if that went beyond the command state, which we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second area where a potential red-card could be applied is over rules of engagement. And the third area is that the -- which is linked to the command state, the national contingent commander could argue that what he's being asked to do goes beyond the mission given to him and the intent of either the multinational commander or the intent of the troop-contributing nation or the national command chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or couldn't he also red-card an illegal -- an unlawful instruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to come on to, Your Honour. Those were what I call the doctrinal areas. And as I stated in my report, that ultimately, if he felt what he was going to be asked to do was illegal, he, on that basis, could say, I'm not prepared to carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it, then, that the question that I asked you with regard to red-carding was a bit off, really, then.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was useful to clarify, for the Court, the term "red-carding," but I'm not quite sure I've quite understood the link between your first question and the red-carding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's the issue of -- let me withdraw the question, because I think in your explanation of red-carding, you've taken us -- you've taken us to an explanation that is of help and does -- and does, in another way, clarify what I was thinking about, without going into it any further. We've talked about one aspect of a tool of war, which is deception. And another aspect of operating within the military is the importance of secrecy; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And as more normally termed within the military, operation security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when talking about military secrecy or, as you've put it, operation security, now that is a feature that exists in every standing army in the world, I would think. Is that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly within my experience, all armed forces will try to protect the security of their operations and plans, and hence a great deal of documentation will be classified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the -- with regard to the issue of the information being classified, using, for example, what we discussed here, which is multinational forces, even in a situation where you have forces that are working together, they independently have operational security issues which are not shared with each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, you're -- you are correct, but I think it would help if I elaborate that within an alliance or coalition, normally you see two types of classification being used. One will be that classification which will be used more generally within the alliance or the coalition; i.e., it is an agreed classification state that is used by all the members of that alliance or coalition, and that will be the general norm. That will be the default setting. If it weren't the default setting, that operation or command structure would not function effectively. But as you've indicated, within that command structure there could be particular classifications, particularly in the intelligence arena, where one or more nations might decide to retain a certain amount of their information and not disclose it to all of their allies or coalition partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is there any particular standard that's used for that or is that something that happens on an ad hoc basis, and by that I mean what is deemed to be practical at the time by that particular army and those particular commanders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are -- to my experience and knowledge, there are -- within the NATO alliance, you'll see classifications states such as "NATO unclassified" or "NATO restricted" or "NATO secret," but in -- within that general alliance framework, I have seen a documentation marked, for example, for US or US and UK eyes only. And I imagine other countries have similar arrangements, but I'm not an expert in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But that would not be an uncommon feature?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your experience, have you come across a situation where a single army broke up into several armies, using the same officers, rules, regulations and laws, both fighting against and with each other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only offer two broad recent historical examples, but may not meet all the conditions of your question. I'm aware, through personal direct experience, and this is maybe where you are heading with the thrust of the question, that the Army of the former Republic of Yugoslavia split into various elements, but another example would be on the break-up of the Soviet Union, elements of the resulting states, and I know with more experience of the Ukraine, for a long time followed quite a lot of the doctrine and procedures of the former Soviet Union, but over time has evolved its own structures and doctrine and has gone its own independent way. But it doesn't meet the condition. They've never been engaged in any but friendly relations with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned, in that, the matter of over time, and I think it would be fair to say - and you would agree - that an institution being built is something that does not happen in a day or even a week, but rather it's something that takes a period of time to develop in its own fullness.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can venture another historical example which may be equally familiar. On the break-up of the British Empire, the armed forces of the sovereign states of the British Commonwealth, for a very long time, followed similar procedures and doctrine, and one can remark today that quite large elements of the Indian and Pakistani Army's structures, doctrine and procedures, are similar to that which the British Army had a good number of years ago. But, again, this is outside my report of command, but I'm relying here on my general knowledge and experience of military affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in regard to that last comment that you have made, those armies, and by that I'm referring to the Indian and Pakistani Army, those are completely independent armies from the British?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the conclusions in your report, sir, and I'm referring to section 4.1, you state: "Although this report refers both to national British and multinational NATO doctrine, the principles are broadly the same. Indeed, it is stated British doctrine that NATO doctrine applies unless separate and specific national direction and guidance is required."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and similar terminology to that is often appended in NATO publications issued within Britain to say -- and it is standard NATO procedure that nations, if they have any reservations to any part of that doctrine, states -- states specifically so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you go on to be really -- in a very specific manner, to identify the parameters of your report, which is something that we talked about a bit yesterday also when we were referring to I believe it's paragraph 2.6, which I will not reiterate at this point in time, but here you say at 4.2: "No attempt has been made to compare UK or NATO doctrine with that of the FRY or Serbia." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the report that we have before us, as you've told us, is a report that deals with an understanding of general principles, mainly defined through NATO glossary, and is generic in nature?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you're signifying that you have no further questions, Mr. Guy-Smith. Just before I hand you over to counsel for the Prosecution to re-examine, Major General, you've just referred to the Army of the former SFRY when asked about an army that breaks up into pieces and then fight amongst one another, against one another, and with each other. What I would like to ask you is: Against the background of your report that deals mainly with multinational forces, how would you characterise the resulting armies that emerged out of the break-up of the SFRY Army in the milieu they found themselves in the period of 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, that's a very big question. Would you please give me a minute or so to get my thoughts together to give the Court a good answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do. Take as much time as you need. I just want an umbrella kind of characterisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm prepared now to offer you an answer to your question, but first of all I would just, for the record, state I'm not an expert on this issue and, therefore, would caveat my answer which is based on my general military knowledge. In answering your question, I would state the following: The Yugoslav National Army was, as its name suggests, a national army that reflected in its composition of members of the various ethnic groups that made together the former Republic of Yugoslavia. On the break-up of the former Republic of Yugoslavia and, hence, of the Yugoslav National Army, the various resulting armies had at least a common tradition and one based on historical developments from 1945 to 1991. Therefore, it is reasonable to suppose that certain aspects of doctrine could and were applied in a similar manner, but that's as far, really, as I'm prepared to go at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just allow me to push you just a little. Would you -- would you regard the emerging armies as a multinational force, or how would you regard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I certainly would not regard them as a multinational force, because they were quite disparate forces. They were no longer operating under a unified command structure. In fact, for much of the time, as I recall, those elements were engaged in combat against each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given that answer that you have just given, to what extent would you say your report is or is not relevant to the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I don't think it's fair to ask whether -- having been invited here, whether my report is relevant or not. I don't think you can, with respect, sir, ask me to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me withdraw the question. If I substituted the word "applicable" for the word "relevant," would you go along with my question? To what extent is your report applicable to the situation that pertained in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Your Honour, that would depend on how -- how the Court wishes to use the information I've provided. What I was asked to do was to provide answers to four questions, specific questions, and in so doing I provided some context to that. And through my knowledge and experience, I gave some context to the medium of NATO and national doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, if I may add - and as I've stated, and both counsels, and you're aware of this - did not in my report to compare and contrast, as it states, I think, paragraph 4.2, with the former Yugoslav command-and-control principles. Had I been asked to do that, I would have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I understand that. And I'm awfully sorry I used the word "relevant" earlier, and I see you take very strong exception to that to the extent it percolates into subsequent questions, and I just want to say I didn't mean to be unfair to you or be unkind to you or to ridicule you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No offence is taken, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what I really do want to understand is, yes, you were given questions to answer, you gave your answers to those questions within a context, and the context you provided was the context of multinational forces. You used NATO and the British Army, together with the Gurkha and French armies and the foreign legions. My only question that I would really like to understand from you is: Within that context of multinational forces, do you see, and if you do, can you tell us how, is -- how are your answers to the questions put to you applicable to this situation, if you're able to help us? If you're not able to help, then you're not able to help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm here to assist the Court, so, Your Honour, I will first of all stress I take no offence from your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and I will do my very best to answer all question from the Court, and that's why I'm here. I think there is two aspects, to answer your question. First of all is of direct applicability. Had I been asked and had the time to write a more comprehensive report, I could have done, and this theoretically, written a much more detailed and lengthy report that would have, as I said, compared and contrasted a wider section of military doctrines and specifically would have, perhaps, looked at the details of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. So that you may regard and I see that as a limitation. But there is a second approach where I believe my report does have a good degree of validity because it provides a standard. It provides a standard through custom of usage being used by a large number of nations over many years, and when particularly one wants to explore the terms "command and control" and how multinational forces operate, which was incumbent on me, I believe those were valid examples to use. Let me try to bring that point to life in another way. In terms of experimentation, one normally applies -- has a standard test applying based on known evidence so that one can compare and contrast this when one's looking at new experimental methods. I just try to make the point, I don't think it's invalid to look at NATO command and control or at British national doctrine when one's asked some questions about command and control. It is up to others and the Court to assess, not I, its validity in relation to this present case. I was acutely aware of that fact and pointed out that limitation in my report, and specifically made very clear those limitations which were clear to me on a normal professional basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand what you say, and I just want to reassure you once again that there is no measure of suggestion on my part that there is no validity in your report. There is absolute validity in it, and my only -- what I'm trying to do here, I'm trying to take lessons from your report to be able to use those lessons in the task that is placed before me. And I appreciate that you mentioned the limitations in your report, but I'm asking you -- let me back off. I also appreciate that you didn't go into as much detail as you otherwise would have had you been asked to do, and I'm just asking you, as you stand there, in a sentence to tell us, given the apparent difference in context -- and let me tell you what I mean there. When you talked about the multinational forces in your report, you talked about forces that are cooperating. You have mentioned that the forces in the former Yugoslavia were not cooperating or were fighting amongst themselves, and I'm saying: Given those two different contexts, how would you suggest to the Court it applies and uses your answers to the questions in this situation, which seems to be so dissimilar, almost contradictory, from the one that you describe in your report? And if you are able to help there, I would appreciate it. If you are not, please say you're not able to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think, well, Your Honour, I'm prepared to, as I say, answer all questions, again bearing in mind my general knowledge and experience. I believe that there are a great deal of aspects of my report that have general validity. For example, in the command model which I described, though it may not be doctrinally defined in identical terms across all armies, but by primary functions, I think it is reasonably fair to propose that a commander has to make decisions, he has to lead and inspire his force, and he has to control his force, as we discussed yesterday. So I think when it comes, in particular, to the control function, I believe the Court should be able to use the information I've proposed in my report and analyse the various actions which are being presented towards this case. But I have no knowledge of the detail, but I suggest that one could use that, in particular, as a useful starting point, because I believe that applies to a national contingent or national force and is not particular to a multinational context which you are making the point is quite distinctive from the one that -- that which pertained during the break-up and subsequent conflict with the former Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thank you very much, and once again your answers are very much appreciated. And I repeat, no offence was ever intended. Mr. Saxon, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I can take a moment to get the podium, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, I think to start I will focus on the discussion that you just had with Judge Moloto. And you told the Chamber that the -- in your view, the emerging armies of the former Yugoslavia that emerged following the break-up were not a multinational force; they were quite a disparate force because they fought each other. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At times, they were engaged in combat against each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General Melvin, you're basing this comment on your general knowledge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're not basing that comment on your specific knowledge of the specific facts of this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say that these forces fought each other, again from your general knowledge and recollection, which forces were fighting each other after the break-up?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I find myself in somewhat of an awkward position because Mr. Saxon is engaged, I guess, in a redirect that has taken into account your questions, Your Honour, as opposed to dealing with my cross-examination, although I know obviously that questions asked by the Chamber can generate questions from the parties. However, in the manner that Mr. Saxon is presently questioning the general, it seems that he is now engaged in impeaching his own witness, and I'm not clear as to whether or not that is appropriate based either on the questions that you have asked nor certainly on my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a prohibition of counsel asking questions arising from the Judges' questions, even questions that were asked while either the witness was testifying either in-chief or in cross, because the Bench intervenes at any stage, and at any stage after intervening, counsel is entitled to ask questions arising from those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. That's why I wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am also not under the impression that there is an attempt to impeach. On the contrary, I see an attempt to clarify. But you and I are guessing here until the next or subsequent questions have been asked. We will be able to say whether there was an impeachment or a clarification, but I seem to be seeing a clarification, rather than an impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. That's why when I started my remarks, I said I find myself in a somewhat of an awkward position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was, in fact, a very awkward position, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I thank you for your guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, General Melvin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that the forces that arose after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia fought each other, to your knowledge and recollection, which forces were fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I recall, and as is stated in my curriculum vitae, I had a short period of operational service in the -- in the Balkans in 1995 and returned on a number of occasions to visit that operational theatre, and also in Kosovo. There were three principal parties to that conflict. There were predominantly Serb-based forces, there were Bosniak Muslim-based forces, and there were largely Croatian-based forces. I do not have precisely, as I once did, the defined names of those forces in my head. I have -- I think I have some of them in my head, but that's as far as I can recollect at this point in time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, going back to your initial response to His Honour Judge Moloto that these were disparate forces because they fought each other, so the fact that one force fought against another force, is that for you an important criteria in determining whether emerging armies have a multinational character or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think, with respect, we're in danger of confusing ourselves here. What I was -- what I was trying to -- to make clear to the Chamber was that on the break-up of the former Republic of Yugoslavia, the various military elements split up according largely to their ethnic divide. They had a common tradition, had common doctrine, and to a large extent had common -- had common weapons. They were disparate, first and foremost, because they were no longer under a unified command structure of the Yugoslav national army. That -- they were never a multinational force because it was a unified national army. The fact -- I was illustrating the point that they were no longer -- they could not be regarded as a multinational force because they were fighting each other. And by -- I think by common and self-definition, you can't have a multinational force fighting each other, I mean, because it's no longer a multinational force, it's a force -- it is no longer that -- a case. But I don't think one can extend my point to provide a general condition or general requirement for not being a multinational -- multinational force, the issue of fighting. I think, with respect, Counsel, you've taken -- taken my words a bit far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then let me try to simplify things, if I can. If emerging armies, by contrast, work together, support each other in common objectives, might that be one consideration in determining whether it's a multinational force or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- if they were working together to commonly agreed-to objectives, then some aspects of their actions and behaviour could be regarded that they would be acting in a multinational manner. But, again, as I've said in my report, one needs to clarify the specific context, and within a coalition, as I think I've quoted in one of the -- the books I've used, there is a very wide spectrum of cooperation in a multinational force. One can have a very close cooperation, bound by law and rules and regulations, such as NATO, or one can have a much looser, ad-hoc coalition, where parties come together purely for very pragmatic reasons, and that coalition can be very -- of short duration. So, again, the time factor can be relevant, but is not the only condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on, General, to a different topic. Today, in response to a question from my colleague, Mr. Guy-Smith, you described a concept called "unity of effort." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I hope I jotted down your definition correctly. What I wrote down was: "Unity of effort is necessary to ensure that the actions of a joint, combined, or multinational force are directed toward a common aim or common objective." Have I caught the essence of your definition correctly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly. It is -- what I've said I don't believe matches word for word the NATO lexicon, but if -- to assist you and the Court, I'm prepared to elaborate further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. General, is what I've just read back to you, is that a broadly accurate --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly, broadly so, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. My question, then, is: Does unity of effort by parties to a multinational force require planning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say -- as I said in an earlier answer to the other counsel, that unity of command and unity of effort go together, and unity of effort does require a degree, and sometimes a very close degree, of cooperation over planning. Without cooperation, without combined planning, it is highly unlikely that you will achieve a unity of effort. One of the ways in which you achieve that unity of effort is through the unity of command, so they are linked in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Later on in -- during your cross-examination today, you explained to my colleague that when assessing information -- when a commander is assessing information, it is important to use as many sources as possible, with a particular emphasis on intelligence sources. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I know we've used this phrase, I guess, quite a bit yesterday, "modern army." For a commander of a modern army, would international news reporting about events that the commander's forces are participating in, might that be a source of information for his or her use?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a general sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And suppose that the commanding officer hears from either local news reports or international news reports that his forces are engaged in crime. What duty would that commander have?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have a duty of -- of initiating an investigation to get to the facts of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct our attentions to some discussion that you had with Mr. Guy-Smith yesterday, General Melvin. First of all, this is at page 9406 of the transcript, lines 20 to 23, Mr. Guy-Smith had asked you about your use of the word "normally," and this is what you said: "I've used the word 'normally' both in my report and in my testimony because, as the Court will have noted, that my report is based both on doctrine and on my understanding borne of experience." And then you say this: "And either doctrine --" or at least this is what the transcript says: "And either doctrine nor experience can account for all eventualities." My question for you is: Did you use the word "either" in that last sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just seeing it coming up on the screen now. If I said "either" there, either I spoke badly or it's been badly quoted. I think it is fair - and the Court will understand - that the sentence should be "neither doctrine, nor experience, can account for all eventualities." I think this is either a simple slip of my tongue or a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And at page 9407 of the transcript, lines 3 to 13, and again in a discussion with Mr. Guy-Smith, you said that you drew your conclusions and information in your report from NATO national doctrine and your experience with the British armed forces and within NATO. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you is: To your knowledge, how many states participate in NATO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 9409 of the transcript of yesterday, lines 20 through 23, in response to a question from Mr. Guy-Smith about mercenaries and the definition of the term "mercenary" that you provide in footnote 16 of your report, you said: "I included this to make it clear that I was referring to the legitimate secondment of individuals from Nation A to Nation B and not -- and, therefore, not anything that could be confused with mercenary." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, very simply, when you refer to the "legitimate secondment of individuals" from the army of Nation A to Nation B, which individuals are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about here the secondees. I'm talking about individuals that are posted or seconded from their home nation state to another state. I had in particular mind when I wrote that passage, because I'm familiar with the example, of soldiers and officers of the British armed forces being seconded to the armed forces of the Sultan of Oman, as a good example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So what you were referring to when you refer to the legitimate secondment of individuals from the army of Nation A to Nation B would include soldiers and officers of the army of Nation A; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Their secondment is authorised by their home nation and contributing -- contributing nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please take a look at what has been marked for identification P2772.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this is your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to paragraph 3.1.6, please. 3.1.6 should be on page 11 in the English e-court version, and if we could go to the same page in the B/C/S version, please, and if we go back to page 10 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.1.6 introduces the subject of mercenaries, but the first two sentences read thusly: "The least formal method of cooperation is the recruiting of individuals of one nation (and hence nationality) by another, which is tolerated, if not encouraged, by the individual's sending nation. Within the British Army, for example, recruits comprise individuals across the whole of Ireland, Nepal (the Gurkhas) and from the member states of the Commonwealth." Have you been following me, General?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, must members of the army of a nation always be citizens of that nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't quite follow your question. What are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in this paragraph, you're talking about the British Army recruiting, amongst others, individuals across the whole of Ireland, people from Nepal, et cetera, and my question, then, is: Must members of the army of a nation always be citizens of that nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, but I would wish to draw your attention to the whole area of citizenship. But my experience, and I'm not legally trained in this matter, is a very complex area, but I can inform the Court that Gurkha soldiers, on retiring from the British Army, now have rights of citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General, though, that means implied in your answer is that those same Gurkha soldiers, while they're serving with the British Army, are not necessarily citizens of the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may not have relinquished their citizenship, as far as I understand. Again, this is a very complex area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And going back to your testimony from yesterday about the legitimate secondment, very simply, must the individuals seconded from the army of Nation A to the army of Nation B always be citizens of Nation A?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's a very hypothetical question. I broadly, broadly said I would suggest the answer to that is, Yes, but I don't think I could exclude all -- all eventualities or other possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So it's possible that they might -- that individuals seconded from the army of Nation A to the army of Nation B might not be citizens of Nation A; it's possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you'd have to have, in this case, two conditions --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you just tell me, yes or no, is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think he should be allowed to answer the question, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, it's not a simple yes-or-no answer here. The -- a number of conditions would have to be met. For example, if an individual had been recruited, let's say an individual from Nepal, as a Gurkha, had been recruited into the British Army, so he is a citizenship -- citizen still of Nepal, he's now in the British Army, and let's say he puts himself forward and volunteers for a secondment post to another State B. Let's take Oman, for example. So in that theoretical example, you could have the condition you are describing, but I do not know whether it's a practical example, I do not know whether it's ever happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not privy to the arrangement between Britain and Nepal on what Britain may or may not do with Nepalese soldiers serving in the British Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in -- not in great detail. All I researched for this report was the raw statistics. I know in my own experience, Your Honour, having dealt with it in my previous appointment, the stationing issues of Gurkha soldiers in Germany, for example, is a complicated issue, so I'm familiar with some aspects of this, but I -- but, again, it is a complicated area which we have expert staffs dealing on these very complicated issues of citizenship and right of access into various countries, and, indeed, on any following-on issues of -- of secondment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further -- excuse me. I may have one further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps one final question for you, General. You were talking today, on cross-examination and then just a moment ago as well, about the concept of unity of command and unity of effort. Can you explain how the concept of unity of command would apply to a seconded force where the national commander of the sending state retains full command, but at the same time the commander of the receiving state has operational command or operational control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no general contradiction here. The unity of command within an alliance or coalition or multinational context is already within that framework where it is understood that nations retain the full command. The unity of command applies as a general principle to provide cohesion in the planning and conduct of operations, and it applies generally across command states and rules of engagement, so it is a -- it's a principle. If -- and it's laid out and explained in NATO doctrine along those lines, and in fact it is quoted in one of the exhibits taken into the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are no further questions from the Bench. That brings us to the end of your testimony, Mr. -- I beg your pardon, Major General Melvin. Thank you so much for taking the time off to come and testify before the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down, and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's been an honour to be here to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to have any witness for this afternoon, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we discuss issues of witnesses, we still have exhibits that have been marked for identification, and I believe there will be some discussion. Perhaps we should take the first break now and then come back, and I believe the parties will have some arguments to provide to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would move for the admission of the following materials that have been marked for identification: This is P2772, which is the expert report of General Melvin; P2773, the allied joint publication doctrine at footnotes 8 and 10 of the report; P2774, the ADP land operations publication at footnotes 9 and 17 of the report; P2775, the British Army doctrine publication called "ADP, Volume 2, Command," at footnote 11 of the report; P2776, NATO document known as "AAP-6" referred to at footnotes 18 to 21 of General Melvin's report; and P2777, the excerpt from the United Kingdom Manual of Military Law referred to at footnote 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. We would object to the admission of the report and the supporting documents to that report that have just been listed by Mr. Saxon. I'm not going to spend time going through the history of the Prosecution's various rendering or submissions of experts before this Chamber. I'm sure the Chamber is well aware of that history and of the varied individuals and reports that theoretically were going to be involved with regard to this particular issue. I would point out two specific matters because I think they are of some importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the importance there, obviously, being the warning back a number of years ago, over three years ago, that generic reports would not be availing. On the 17th of September in this year, this Chamber issued its decision with regard to the Prosecution's motion to substitute expert witnesses, something that, as the Chamber's aware of, the Defence resisted for the reasons that have previously been mentioned. And of importance, this Chamber said, at paragraph 7: "The Trial Chamber notes that Major General Melvin's anticipated evidence relates to the interrelationship between the VJ, VRS, and SVK, and the accused's authority over members of these armies, key issues in the present case. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that this evidence is prima facie relevant and of probative value." The testimony that you have heard from Major General Melvin, coupled with the remarks that he made in his report, are very clear. In paragraph 2.4, he says: "The approach taken in this report when answering the four questions are considered a general context of command rather than specific. In so doing, I provide some background doctrinal material on command drawn from the United Kingdom and NATO sources. It is important to note that I make no attempt whatsoever to refer to the specific matters raised in the indictment of Colonel General Momcilo Perisic, nor do I try to 'get into his mind' (and his decision-making) in providing some form of commentary based on speculation on his understanding of his responsibilities, including his adoption of Yugoslav command-and-control doctrine procedures."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just said could I just interrupt you for a while, and I have requested that we move into closed session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At paragraph 2.6 of his report, entitled "Limitation on Conclusions," the general states: "I offer only the most general of conclusions, noting that I am not qualified to provide, within this expert witness report, detailed observations, let alone conclusions, on the specifics of the case against Momcilo Perisic." And, of course, as we discussed late in his testimony today, in his report he makes it very clear at section 4.2: "No attempt has been made to compare UK or NATO doctrine with that of the FRY or Serbia. It has not been possible to research this matter in sufficient detail within the time available to the author of this expert report." I would note one other matter because I think it's of some importance with regard to a full and complete understanding of what the report is based on. At paragraph 1.3, in discussing his journey to writing this report, he says, in the middle of the paragraph: "Mr. Saxon agreed and sent me the next day (3 September 2009) a revised list of four 'general' questions for answer by Monday, 21 September 2009, set out below in section 1.6 which would not, in his view, require a detailed examination of the documentation pertaining to the case. I was encouraged, however, to read into this material handed over to me in the form of a CD-ROM, should I have time, after completing my expert report." So not only is it clear that the report is one which is general in nature, generic in nature, clearly in contradiction to an admonition given several years ago by this Chamber or the Chamber seized with the matter. He has made it very clear in his report that he is neither qualified to deal with the specific issues that were germane to this Chamber's decision of the 17th of September, and I believe that the question and answers between, most specifically, the Chamber and the gentleman pointed out the very difficulties that this report presents for purposes of its introduction and its reliance, because there is virtually no ability to apply it in any way or other than the most general of senses. And in that regard, it is, in our respectful submission, not worthy of admission because, in large measure, it will not assist the Chamber with regard to the issues that it identified specifically concerning the relationship of the various identified military armies. Once again, I include in the report -- when I object to the report, I include the materials that were in support of that, because I look at the entirety of this as being one package as opposed to parsed out sequentially. That is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you sit down, Mr. Guy-Smith, you make a very subtle concession at the end and you say -- give me time. You say, at page 37, line 3 -- line 3, you say "other than the most general of senses." Is it your submission that that most general of senses wouldn't be perhaps the extent to which it could be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's always the difficulty in being, I think, as honest as possible and as candid as possible with regard to one's argument. I can see, in a very general fashion, some limited potential. So with regard to your question, to answer your question directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- because I know you want a direct answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- my answer would be that there is a limited value, in the theoretical sense. We're dealing with it in an abstract fashion. But I rely upon and I fall back upon the guidance that the Chamber gave in the first instance in its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. The Chamber may have given its guidance in the first instance, without the hindsight of the content of the specific report, to be able to determine whether or not there is even a general sense in which the report could be useful, and I'm saying if, indeed, we concede that in that very limited general sense it could be used, is this now a question of weight? There may be very little weight to attach. I'm not suggesting there is or there isn't. But just following your argument and taking, for argument's sake, for the time being that your argument is acceptable, then the weight that would be given to the report would be to the extent of its helpfulness in that very general sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, dealing with it as a theoretical matter, I would agree with what you've said. If we were only dealing with it as a theoretical matter and only as an abstract matter, then the answer would most definitely have to be, of necessity, yes. The question of weight would come in, and obviously I would at that point say it has little if no weight whatsoever. But I'm arguing actually more vigorously than that at this time, and the reason for that is because the man has told us, and with all due respect to what his knowledge may be, that he never focused on the issue as presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, I think there is a very good possibility, and this is with a full recognition that the Chamber is not only insightful but incisive with regard to the information that's presented to it, that it will be in a position where it's looking at information that essentially becomes irrelevant to its considerations, because there are -- there are, in fact, without a doubt, questions that arise concerning the very matters the Chamber alluded to in its decision that have not been answered by this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's understood, Mr. Guy-Smith. Let's bear in mind that we're dealing here with an expert witness, not a fact witness. And if we wanted the expert witness to pronounce specifically on the facts of the case as an expert, then he should have been given the facts of the case, and he would have pronounced on them as an expert. That was not done, and what was done was, Come and give us what a general idea would be -- general answers to the questions that are being put to you. And it is for the Chamber then to extrapolate from those answers, whatever it finds applicable to the facts of the case, to extrapolate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I can't -- I can't in any fashion whatsoever, in good faith, argue with you on a theoretical level. There's no way for me to do that, nor would I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I'm not talking -- you see, this is the thing. You lose me when you talk about it's a theoretical abstract -- on a theoretical level itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see what -- I see where I'm not being clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm dealing with a practical level. I'm just saying that to the extent where it gives generalities, the Chamber could use those generalities to guide itself and, of course, would bear in mind the fact that the report is not intended to comment specifically on the facts of this case. That's why he was not given the facts of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, but he was given the facts of the case. That's what I'm -- that's what I'm telling you. The CD-ROM that he was given included information about the facts of the case that he chose not to review because of pressure of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he was told not to look at that, and he can look at it later, if he's interested. But, I mean, whatever he says, he says he didn't use the CD-ROM for purposes of this report. He gave a report in response to the questions put to him, as he understands them generally. Now, I understand that it is not on all fours with the facts of the case. That I understand, but I'm saying to the extent that there are general principles that can be extrapolated from it, wouldn't it be of some assistance to the Chamber to that extent?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to a general principle, if there is a general principle that the Chamber is not aware of or familiar with that requires reliance upon an expert's opinion, my answer, of necessity, to that question would have to be, Yes, because that would be a responsible answer to the question, I mean, if that's the manner in which the question is being -- being asked. And I don't have any other way of answering that question, to be perfectly honest with you, Your Honour, but to say, Yes. If there's some conceivable help that it could be to you, then I want you to have that conceivable help. I mean, that I would agree with. I don't think it would either be prudent or responsible as an advocate, no matter what my position may be, to say anything other than that. I'm taking -- as I'm saying, I'm taking a more strident position here, because I, as you said, it's not on all fours. I don't think it's even -- we're even on a unicycle with regard to this particular report, and part of the difficulty is the models that have been put forth in the abstract may have some theoretical basis upon which reflection can be had, but they also have the potential of being confusing because they have not been tied in to the fact-specific questions that this Chamber needs to decide, which is part of the reason why I keep on pushing the fact issue. Having said that, I understand your position, and I don't want to say, Yes, and you know I don't want to say, Yes, but if I'm being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you say, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, but I do say, Yes, in terms of the manner in which you frame the question, because otherwise -- otherwise I would be incredible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How else would you like me to phrase my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, in only the most honest way that you think of it and the most honest way that I can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can assure you that you can trust the Chamber not to be confused. I heard you say -- suggesting that the report might just add some confusion, but I just want you to understand that the Chamber would not be confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I -- when the word came into my mind, I was a little concerned about using it in any event, and I meant no disrespect whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you did. I'm just reassuring you that you can trust the Chamber not to be confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we agreed now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We are -- we are -- I guess, we are agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I need to ask Mr. Saxon to reply, if he wants to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based upon where the Court is thinking, I think the answer is, No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- because I believe you've been pretty clear about what your thinking is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I tried not to show my hand. If I've been so callous, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think you were more guiding than showing a hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I like your diplomacy, and I appreciate it. Thank you so much. Well, then, given that it will then be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of completeness, I would like to raise an administrative matter now, in case that affects your decision and in case counsel wants to say anything about it. There remains the outstanding question of the additional assignment that you directed General Melvin to perform yesterday, and he has -- moments ago, he has communicated to the Prosecution that he would need approximately three weeks to do a short report based on the direction that you gave to him. He might need to engage the assistance of others. And so I wanted to make sure that that knowledge is on the table before any final decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any comment on that, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It seems to me that with regard to the directions made by the Chamber, that would be a subsequent -- a subsequent secondary report, and in the event that an examination need be on that report, that would be an entirely different matter. I can see them as being distinct issues, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thought so, too. Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Does that then dispose of that part of the business?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any other business to raise with the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber has some business to raise. Just in case I wasn't clear, the admission of the report includes the associated documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just an oral decision on some motion that's been outstanding for some time. Just to make sure, we are in public session, aren't we? Thank you so much. On the 19th of October, 2009, the Prosecution filed its notice withdrawing Prosecution submission on decision on Prosecution's first Bar table motion of the 5th of October, 2009, and filing of a corrected version, hereinafter referred to as the "19th of October notice" whereby it addressed several issues pertaining to the Chamber's decision on Prosecution's first Bar table motion of the 5th of October, 2009, hereinafter referred to as the "5th October decision." The Trial Chamber hereby decides as follows: 1. The Trial Chamber notes that in its 5th October decision, it admitted several documents under the condition that the revised translation be provided by the Prosecution. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution, in its 19th of October notice, submits that the relevant translations are now up-loaded to e-court and thus confirms that the following documents are now part of the trial record, under seal: Rule 65 ter numbers 09480, 09486, 09492, 09497, and 09499. 2. The Trial Chamber notes that the 19th October notice specifies the exact portions of the two voluminous items which the Prosecution seeks to be admitted. The Trial Chamber is satisfied as to the relevance and probative value of the following: Rule 65 ter number 09567, pages 12 to 15, 33, 53 to 54, 79 to 80, 209 to 215, and 229 to 230. As a consequence, the above-mentioned portions are admitted into evidence, under seal. Similarly, the Trial Chamber admits into evidence, under seal, the following portions of the video marked as Rule 65 ter number 09562; that is, at 20 minutes 49 seconds to 21 minutes 33 seconds, 27 minutes 42 seconds to 28 minutes 11 seconds, and 46 minutes 49 seconds to 47 minutes 55 seconds. May I just pause here. I know there is too much detail here. You can be provided with a document detailing this at the end. I see you struggling very hard to write, and you're asking your colleague there, Mr. Guy-Smith, whether he's following what I'm saying. You'll get the document. Okay? 3. The Trial Chamber notes that the 19th October notice submits that the full translations of the relevant pages of Rule 65 ter number 07305 have been up-loaded to e-court. The Trial Chamber is satisfied as to their relevance and probative value, and therefore admits pages 7 and 10 of this exhibit, under seal. 4. The Trial Chamber finds that the B/C/S versions of Rule 65 ter numbers 09481, 09513, and 09540, up-loaded to e-court, are now sufficiently legible. The Trial Chamber also notes that the 19 October notice submits that the revised translations have now been up-loaded to e-court. The Trial Chamber finds that 65 ter numbers 09481, 09513, and 09540 are relevant and of probative value. They are, therefore, admitted into evidence, under seal. 5. Finally, the Trial Chamber notes that the 19 October notice submits under 65 ter numbers 09468 and 09469 should be treated confidentially. The Trial Chamber orders that these documents be placed under seal. That's the end of the decision. Can I suggest that parties be given copies of this oral decision, because it's just too complicated. Thank you so much. That's the end of the business. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness of the Prosecution is scheduled to testify on Monday, 2nd of November, so we ask that we adjourn until Monday, 2 November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Do you know what time we are sitting on Monday and in which court?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you give me about 10 seconds, Your Honour, I think I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar is going to be able to help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told it's in the morning, in Courtroom II. Then, in that event, the case stands adjourned to Monday, the 2nd of November, at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: WITNESS:  ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN [Resumed]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.37 p.m.,
